studies.title: Sacred Signs And Old Grudges
studies.meaning: A list of things not to violate, all of them markers rather than rules: the rites themselves, the sacred month, the offering animals, the garlands hung on them to show what they were, and the people travelling towards the House. Each is a sign that something stands under protection. The ayah then turns to the feeling that would make a person ignore such a sign. Old hatred is named and refused, and cooperation is defined by what it is for.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from one of the last surahs revealed. The reference to being barred from the Sacred Mosque points back to the year the Muslims were turned away at Hudaybiyya without performing the pilgrimage. Within a few years the same people who had turned them back would be travelling under their protection. The ayah speaks into that window, when the grievance was recent and the power had shifted.

keyTerms.note: From a root for perceiving and for a mark that makes something recognisable. The word covers both the rites and the physical signs by which they were known, which is why animals and months appear in one list.
Necklaces of bark or hide hung on an animal set aside for offering. They worked as public notice: anyone seeing the collar knew that the beast and the person driving it were not to be touched.
A word for lasting dislike rather than a flare of anger. It names a grudge that has had time to become part of a person, and it recurs in the ayah about testimony a few lines later.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sacred months were the economy's breathing space. For four months a year weapons were put down across Arabia, and the great fairs ran under that truce, with poetry contests, debt settlements and marriage arrangements all timed to it. A collared animal walking a trade road was untouchable. Breaking any of these conventions did not merely offend; it made travel impossible for everyone.
studies.didYouKnow: The warning about letting hatred for a people carry you into wrongdoing appears twice in this surah, here and six ayat later, each time applied differently: once to aggression against those who barred the way, once to the giving of fair testimony. Repetition this close together is unusual, and the commentators read the second as generalising the first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates a grievance from its expression without denying the grievance. The people who barred them are described as having done exactly that, so the wrong is acknowledged in the same sentence that refuses to license retaliation. Cooperation is then defined by content rather than by loyalty: the question asked of any alliance is what it is for, which cuts across the tribal assumption that you help your own.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same warning about hatred, applying it to the giving of testimony.
Describes the barring from the Sacred Mosque that this ayah refers back to.
Sets the limit of hostility, allowing kindness towards those who did not fight you.

studies.applyIt: Think of one person you deal with while carrying an old grievance, and check whether the grievance has started deciding small things: how quickly you reply, whether you pass on information they need. Fix one of those this week without announcing it. The concern here is not the feeling but what the feeling has quietly begun to authorise.

studies.title: Justice Is Nearer To Awe
studies.meaning: The instruction arrives with its own obstacle attached. Hatred of a people is named as the pressure that bends judgement, and the ayah does not ask for the hatred to be resolved first. It repeats the command bare, then gives a comparative rather than an absolute: acting justly is nearer to consciousness of God. The commentators note the modesty of that phrasing, which measures an act by its direction of travel instead of declaring it sufficient.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a late surah, in a passage that begins with the standing of agreements and moves through the treatment of those hostile to the community. Relations with several groups had broken down by this point, after years of raids and broken terms. The commentators record no single occasion, and read the warning as addressed to a community that now had the power to be unfair.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word whose root meaning is presence. A witness is one who was there, so testimony is described as reporting what you actually have rather than as advocacy for a side.

From the root for balancing two weights. The same consonants can also mean to turn aside, so the word holds equity and deviation together, which the ayah exploits by commanding one and warning of the other.

A comparative, not a superlative. Just conduct is placed nearer to awareness of God than the alternative rather than identified with it, which keeps the statement measured and leaves room for the difficulty.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony in Arabia was a communal act. Witnesses were not strangers but the men of a clan, and their word carried the weight of the group behind it, which meant an honest witness could be accused of betraying his own people. Feuds ran for decades and everyone could recite the injuries. Being asked to testify accurately about a tribe that had killed your relatives was not an abstract test.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and 4:135 form a pair, and the pairing is exact. Each begins by calling believers to stand, each names a temptation, and the two temptations are opposites: one warns against being pulled by affection for yourself and your family, this one against being pushed by hatred of an enemy. Between them they cover both directions a witness can lean.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Justice is presented as something that survives enmity, which means it does not depend on the other party deserving it. The passage assumes a settled hostility and asks for accuracy anyway, decoupling fairness from goodwill. Calling it nearer to awareness of God rather than identical with it makes a further point: the act is no substitute for an inner state, but it is the closest thing available to a person who is not there yet.

crossReferences.why: States the same demand with its terms reversed, naming desire rather than hatred as the pressure.
Uses the identical warning about hatred a few ayat earlier, applied to retaliation.
Extends fairness to those who have not fought you, describing God as loving the equitable.

studies.applyIt: Pick a person or a group whose views reliably irritate you and find one thing they have got right. Say it plainly, without the softening clause that takes it back. You are not endorsing anything. The ayah assumes the dislike stays and asks only that it stop editing what you are willing to admit is true.

studies.title: As If He Killed Everyone
studies.meaning: The ayah reports a decree given to the Children of Israel, drawn as the conclusion of the story told a few lines earlier. A single life is equated with all lives in both directions, killing and saving. The exceptions named keep the statement from becoming a claim that no killing is ever answered, and the commentators read the comparison as concerning the character of the act: what a murderer does to one person he has shown himself willing to do to anyone.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a late surah. The passage follows the account of the first murder, where one brother kills the other over an offering, and the decree is introduced as the consequence drawn from it. Much of the surah at this point addresses communities holding earlier scriptures, and the ayah reports what was written for them before adding that many afterwards went to excess in the land.

keyTerms.note: The verb for writing, used of what is inscribed and settled. Applying it to a moral statement given to an earlier community presents it as recorded and standing, not as advice offered once and left.

keyTerms.gloss: as though, it is as if
keyTerms.note: A particle of comparison, and its presence is the whole grammar of the ayah. What follows is stated as a likeness rather than an equivalence, which is how the classical commentators handle the scale of it.
The causative of the verb to live. Commentators take it to cover rescuing from death and also lifting someone out of ruin, so the counterpart to killing is any act that restores a person to living.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a society organised around blood vengeance, one killing was never one killing. A death obliged a clan to answer, the answer obliged the other side, and a single incident at a well could set two groups killing each other for a generation. Everyone listening had heard the genealogies of such feuds recited aloud. The claim that one murder amounted to all murders described something they had watched happen.
studies.didYouKnow: The comparison here has a close parallel in rabbinic literature, in the Mishnah's charge to witnesses in capital cases, where saving a single life is likened to saving a whole world. The Quran presents the statement as something decreed for the Children of Israel, and the two texts stand as independent witnesses to one formulation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah refuses arithmetic in moral judgement. If a life could be weighed against a number, killing one person would be a smaller wrong than killing many, and the comparison denies exactly that by making a single death total. Placing the saving clause in the same sentence gives the reverse an equal scale, so ordinary rescue is not a lesser category of act but the opposite pole of one measure.

crossReferences.why: Tells the story of the two brothers from which this decree is drawn.
States the sanctity of life directly and sets a limit on the response of an heir.
Places the prohibition of killing among the commands given to every community.

studies.applyIt: Take the news you read this week and find one number in it, a count of people affected by something. Look up a single name from among them if you can, and read that one story instead. The ayah works by refusing to let a person become a figure, and the smallest way to keep it is to make the figure a person again.

studies.title: Repentance Before The Arrest
studies.meaning: An exception is carved out of a severe passage, and its timing carries the weight: repentance counts if it comes before the person is caught. Once capture has happened a change of heart is indistinguishable from surrender, so the window is placed while the choice still costs something. The ayah after it turns from the offender to everyone, asking for awareness of God and for a means of drawing near, which the commentators read as any act that closes distance.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a passage about violent robbery and its consequences, itself following the account of the first murder. The commentators connect the surrounding ayat with a group who committed a killing after being given hospitality, though the reports vary in detail. What the exception clause records is that the severity was published together with the way out of it, in the same breath.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to return, and it is used of God turning towards a person as well as of a person turning towards God. One word describes both movements, which is why the two are hard to separate.
From the root for capacity and for measuring out. The clause turns on the moment power passes to the other side, so the timing of the repentance is defined by who now holds the situation.

A word for the connection or path by which one reaches something wanted. The commentators explain it broadly as whatever brings a person nearer to God, and note that the term is left deliberately open.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Highway robbery was the standing danger of caravan travel. The roads between Mecca, Medina and the north ran through country where a small band could take a season's trade in an afternoon, and there was no policing beyond what a clan could mount for itself. A man who had robbed a caravan lived outside anyone's protection until he was caught. The window described here was a real one.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the means of approach occurs in the Quran only twice, here and in surah 17, where it describes those already close to God competing to come nearer still. The two uses place the same term at opposite ends of a scale, once for someone looking for a way back and once for those who have arrived.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Mercy is given a deadline rather than a limit, which is a particular kind of seriousness. The offer stands while it can still be refused, and closing it at the moment of capture keeps repentance from becoming a tactic. The second ayah then removes any suggestion that this is a special provision for offenders: the same movement towards God is asked of everyone, in identical language, immediately afterwards.

crossReferences.why: Sets the same kind of limit, contrasting repentance in time with repentance at the point of death.
Uses the same word for the means of approach, of those already near to God.
Offers those who stop what has already passed, on the same condition of ceasing first.

studies.applyIt: If there is something you have decided to stop doing when circumstances eventually force you to, try moving the date forward by a week. The ayah makes the value of a turn depend on whether it still cost something when you made it. Nothing about the act changes; what changes is whether it was yours.

studies.title: A People He Loves
studies.meaning: The warning about turning away is answered not with a threat but with a replacement: God will bring a people, described in five clauses. Love is mentioned in both directions and God's love is named first. Then two opposite postures, lowered towards believers and firm towards those who reject, which the commentators read as one disposition adjusted to its object. The last clause is the sharpest of them: they do not fear the blame of anyone who blames.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a late surah, in a passage about alliances and about people whose loyalty ran elsewhere. The commentators record several suggestions about who the promised people are and settle on none, treating the description as the point rather than the identification. The community by this stage was large enough that reputation inside it had become a form of pressure in its own right.

keyTerms.note: A plural of the word for humbled or lowly, used here of a bearing chosen rather than imposed. Commentators explain it as making oneself low for believers, the way ground is low enough to be walked on.
From the root for might and for what is rare and hard to reach. Set against the previous word it describes not harshness but a refusal to be moved, so the pair marks two directions of one strength.

The form names one instance of blame, so what is denied is not endurance under sustained criticism but any flinch at all, including at the single remark that makes a person adjust what they were about to say.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation in Arabia was enforced by poetry. A satirist could damage a man's standing across the peninsula in a few lines that travelled with every caravan, and families paid to have their honour defended in verse. Shame was the main instrument of social control, more effective than any authority. Describing people who do not flinch at blame named something rare enough to be worth promising.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah names five qualities of the promised people, and only one of them concerns their relationship with God directly. The rest describe how they stand towards other human beings: gentle in one direction, immovable in another, and indifferent to criticism. The commentators note that the sequence begins with being loved rather than with anything they do.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Divine love is stated as prior. God loves them, and their love follows in the second clause, which puts the initiative outside the human being. The passage also treats the community as replaceable, which is a hard thing to say to people just warned about defection: the message does not depend on any particular group carrying it. And courage is defined socially, as freedom from the fear of what people will say.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the threat of replacement, saying others would be brought who are not like you.
Makes love the axis of the relationship, tying it to following the Messenger.
Describes those who deliver God's messages and fear none but Him.

studies.applyIt: Notice one thing you did not say this week because of how it would land, and ask whether the reason was kindness or fear of being thought badly of. Those two feel identical from the inside. The ayah names the second one specifically, and the way to tell them apart is usually who was being protected.

studies.title: Nothing To Fear, No Grief
studies.meaning: Four communities are listed by name and then the sentence starts again with a condition that cuts across all of them: whoever believes in God and the Last Day and acts rightly. The commentators discuss the grammar closely, since the listing is taken over by a singular relative clause. What is promised is stated as an absence, no fear and no grief, which are the two directions anxiety runs, forward towards what may come and back over what is gone.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a late surah addressed largely to communities holding earlier scriptures, in a passage that has just told them their books do not stand on nothing. A near-identical sentence appears earlier in the Quran at 2:62. The commentators treat the repetition as deliberate, and note that the placement here follows an appeal rather than a rebuke.

keyTerms.note: A community named three times in the Quran and never described. Classical commentators offer differing identifications and several say plainly that the group is not certainly known, so the name is left standing as given.
Anxiety directed forward, at what has not yet happened. Across the Quran it is paired with a word for grief over what already has, and the two together cover the whole timeline of distress.
The verb for working, joined to a word meaning sound or fit for purpose. Right action is described as repair, making something work as it should, rather than as compliance with an instruction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Religious identity in Arabia was inherited and public, tied to which shrines your people kept and which oaths they swore by. Communities lived side by side in Medina with their own courts, festivals and burial grounds, and a person's group was visible in their name. A sentence that named four communities and then made the same statement about individuals inside them worked against the grain of how everyone was categorised.
studies.didYouKnow: In this ayah the word for the Sabians stands in the nominative case, where the construction would normally require the accusative, as it does at 2:62. It is among the most discussed grammatical features in the Quran, and the classical grammarians explained it as a deliberate suspension that sets the word slightly apart from the list around it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sentence puts the decisive weight on what a person believes and does rather than on the label they carry, without dissolving the labels: the communities are named, not merged. The promise is framed as removal rather than addition, which is a specific kind of comfort. It does not say what such people will be given. It says what will not be there, and names the whole of what human beings are usually afraid of.

crossReferences.why: States the same sentence with the communities in a different order and a reward clause added.
Gives the same promise to whoever submits and does good, in the singular.
Explains why the communities differ, and tells them to compete in good works.

studies.applyIt: Write down the fear that has been running underneath this week, and the regret that has been running alongside it. One sentence each. The ayah names those two and only those two, which suggests that almost everything heavy you are carrying is one or the other, and it helps just to see which.
